So he (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the camel, and the cow, and the sheep, there is no problem.'

key_terms.الدَّوَابّ: al-Dawabb — riding beasts or domesticated animals, particularly those used for transport or agriculture
key_terms.سُؤْر: Su'r — the leftover water or food that an animal or person has drunk or eaten from; a specific term in Islamic jurisprudence regarding ritual purity
key_terms.لَا بَأْس: La ba's — 'no problem' or 'no harm'; a standard jurisprudential phrase indicating permissibility

ai.seo_question: Is the leftover water of camels, cows, and sheep considered ritually pure for drinking and wudu?
ai.summary: Sama'ah ibn Mihran, a direct companion of the Imam, asked about the ritual purity of water that has been drunk by animals. The Imam (peace be upon him) explicitly permitted drinking the leftover water of camels, cows, and sheep, and using it for wudu (ritual ablution), indicating these animals' saliva does not render the water impure (najis). This ruling is consistent with the broader Shia jurisprudential principle that domesticated livestock do not transmit ritual impurity through their saliva.

en.hubeali: Abu Dawood, from Al Husayn Bin Saeed, from his brother Al Hassan, from Zur’at, fro mSama’at who said, ‘I asked himasws, ‘Can one drink something from the residue (of the water drunk by) the animals, and can one perform Ablution (Wudhu) from it?’
So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘As for the camel, and the cow, and the sheep, so there is no problem’.
en.sarwar: 3. Abu Dawud has narrated from al-Husayn ibn Sa‘id from his brother al-Hassan from Zur’ah, from Sama‘ah who has said the following: “I once asked him (the Imam), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, ‘Is it permissible to use for Wudu’ the leftover water from which animals have drunk?’
He (the Imam) replied, ‘As far as the camel, cow and sheep are concerned, it is permissible.’”
